paper.title: Is inequality in subjective well-being meritocratic? Danish evidence from linked survey and administrative data
paper.journal: Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement is printed in the article. …

registers.role: linkage; family characteristics (parent identifiers, divorce, mother age at birth)
variables_mentioned: civil registration numbers of the parents

registers.name_in_paper: historical registers on income, wealth, education, and family composition
registers.years: covering the respondents and their parents from childhood (parental variables measured when the individual was 17-19 years old) up to 2017
registers.role: treatment/controls (parental income, wealth, education; adult income, wealth, education, occupation, family status) and outcomes (income rank in midlife)
variables_mentioned: total income computed by Statistics Denmark (gross income including labor market income, transfers and wealth income)
total wealth computed by Statistics Denmark

registers.name_in_paper: administrative registers [on] school grades of the respondents at the end of compulsory schooling (age 15-16)
registers.years: available for people up to age 32
variables_mentioned: exam grade and teacher assessment in the mandatory courses Math and Danish

registers.name_in_paper: administrative data on unemployment and sickness benefits
registers.role: controls (parental and own unemployment and health shocks)

registers.name_in_paper: a 10 percent random sample of the Danish population
registers.years: 2017 for occupations; by year for municipalities
registers.role: construction of neighborhood and occupation affluence measures
variables_mentioned: average annual income of individuals between 40 and 55 years old living in the municipality
average annual income of individuals between 40 and 55 years old in each occupation in 2017

registers.role: outcome (subjective well-being, Cantril Ladder) and merit proxies (self-control, financial literacy, self-reported GPA for older respondents)

linkages: survey responses linked to administrative registers using civil registration numbers (CPR numbers)
individuals linked to their parents through the civil registration numbers of the parents stored in the population register
invitees (not only participants) linked to register data, which allows the comparison of participants and invited in Table 1
siblings identified within the survey sample for the Appendix B analysis (96 individuals)

sample.universe: A representative sample of 50,000 Danes between 18 and 64 years old, randomly selected by Statistics Denmark with an oversampling of the youngest cohort, invited to the 2018 CEBI online survey through Digital Post
selection_rules: focus on cohorts up to age 55 for whom information on parents during childhood exists in the administrative data
10,464 individuals completed the survey, a response rate of 29 percent
main analyses restricted to two age groups: 18-19 (young adults) and 40-55 (midlife)
baseline samples require non-missing register information on all relevant explanatory variables (3,937 young; 2,903 midlife)
robustness sample includes all respondents, imputing missing register values with the average of the other respondents (4,416 young; 3,523 midlife)
sample.period: survey fielded in 2018; register variables based on 2017 values; parental variables measured when the individual was 17-19 years old
sample.n_observations: 3,937 (age 18-19) and 2,903 (age 40-55) in the baseline regressions; 10,464 completed surveys for cohorts up to age 55
sample.n_individuals: 10,464 survey completers (cohorts up to age 55); 50,000 invited

construction_notes: All continuous variables are transformed into within-cohort fractional ranks from zero to 100; regression estimates are multiplied by 100
Robustness uses ordinal ranks (identical observations assigned distinct ranks randomly) and z-scores instead of fractional ranks
Three-year averages of annual income and wealth are computed for the individual and the parents to reduce temporary variation
Parent income (wealth) is the sum of the average annual income (wealth) for the mother and father over three years when the individual was 17, 18 and 19 years old

Parental unemployment shock: either parent unemployed in the three years around the individual turning 18; parental health shock: either parent received sickness benefits in the five years around the individual turning 18
Own unemployment shock: unemployed within the last three years; own health shock: received sickness benefits within the last five years

GPA is computed from the exam grade and the teacher assessment in the mandatory courses Math and Danish at the end of compulsory schooling (age 15-16); including other courses does not increase the explanatory power
Register GPA exists for respondents up to age 32; self-reported GPA from the survey is used for older respondents (cumulative distributions compared in Fig. A.2 for 905 individuals aged 26-32)
A 2005 reform changed the grading scale (from the 10-grade '13-skalaen' to the 7-grade '7-trins-skalaen'); the authors presume the change did not affect within-cohort rankings

Neighborhood affluence: average annual income of individuals aged 40-55 living in the municipality in a given year, computed on a 10 percent random sample; occupation affluence: analogous by occupation in 2017
Depressed is a dummy for a life satisfaction rank below ten; Very Satisfied is a dummy for a life satisfaction rank above 90
The standard deviation of life satisfaction (0-10 Cantril Ladder) in the sample is 1.65
Confidence intervals for M are bootstrapped with 2,000 replications; standard errors in the regression tables are robust

Weighted-regression robustness uses inverse probability (propensity score) weights based on gender, GPA and all SEB variables for the 19 year-olds, and on gender, age, all SEB variables and adult outcomes for the 40-55 year-olds

claims.statement: Among 18-19 year-olds, a higher parental income rank is associated with a higher life satisfaction rank, conditional on school performance.

register_source.value: 2018 CEBI online survey (Center for Economic Behavior and Inequality, University of Copenhagen); not a register

units.value: percentiles of the outcome rank for a move from the bottom to the top of the regressor's within-cohort rank distribution (rank-rank coefficient multiplied by 100)

units.value: percent of the predicted variation in the outcome attributable to merits orthogonal to SEB

magnitude.interpretation: merits account for at least a quarter of the inequality in life satisfaction and at most a half

key_assumptions.assumption: Selection into the estimation sample (survey participation, 29 percent response rate, and non-missing register information) does not distort the estimates.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Weighted regressions with propensity-score weights (Table 5, panel H) and imputation of missing register data (panel I).

implies_edges.from: Survey participation (response to the 2018 CEBI survey)
implies_edges.to: Meritocratic share of inequality in life satisfaction (M)

key_assumptions.assumption: The survey measures (life satisfaction, self-control, financial literacy, and self-reported GPA for older respondents) are not contaminated by response errors that drive the estimates.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Footnote 1 discusses attenuation and social-desirability bias; Appendix Fig. A.2 compares register and self-reported GPA.

key_assumptions.assumption: Ranking individuals within cohort removes life-cycle and time variation in levels, so that rank-rank coefficients are comparable across ages.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 2.2 motivates the rank transformation (Chetty et al., 2014).

key_assumptions.assumption: The variation in life satisfaction left unexplained by the regression is unrelated to SEB and merits (random circumstances, survey response noise).

ambiguities: The estimate is a variance share, not a signed effect; 'sign: positive' records only that merits/circumstances account for a positive share of the predicted (or total) variation.
No standard error is printed for M; the table reports a bootstrapped 95 percent confidence interval (2,000 replications) where one is given.

value.parameter_of_interest: M
value.normalisation: M is reported in percent; η is the residual from Eq. (3), x = x̄ + cz + η, i.e. the variation in merits orthogonal to SEB

value.claimed_domain: the role of merits relative to SEB for inequality in subjective well-being across countries: Denmark, with very meritocratic institutions, is argued to be close to the maximum / an upper bound
boundary_conditions: Denmark has some of the most meritocratic institutions in the world
free public education, generous student allowances, admission based on previous school performance, taxation of inheritances

outcomes_examined_not_reported: self-assessed impulsivity: examined, 'not signiﬁcantly related to life satisfaction' (p. 340 fn. 10)
self-reported belief in own abilities: related to life satisfaction but excluded as too close to the outcome (p. 340 fn. 10)
experimentally elicited economic preferences: 'Including these preference measures in our analysis does not change the conclusions' (p. 339 fn. 6)
GPA from courses other than Math and Danish: 'Including other courses does not increase the explanatory power' (p. 340)
